sections.body_en:
The time of obligation for all the mitzvot of the Torah begins when the child reaches the age of mitzvot, but before that he is still a minor and the Torah has not obligated him in the mitzvot. However, even before children reach the age of mitzvot, it is a Torah mitzva to teach them Torah, as it is said (Devarim 11:19): "And you shall teach them to your children." And since the first aim of study is to keep and do all the words of the Torah, as it is said (ibid. 5:1): "And you shall learn them and keep them, to do them", the Sages said that together with the mitzva to teach the children Torah, there is an obligation to educate them to fulfil the mitzvot. That is, included in the mitzva of Torah study is becoming accustomed to fulfilling its mitzvot, each mitzva from the time that the child can understand the rules of the mitzva and fulfil it properly (Sukka 42a). It follows that it is a Torah mitzva to teach young children Torah and to accustom them to keeping the mitzvot, but the obligation of actually fulfilling each and every mitzva is rabbinic. In any case we have learned that the most important foundation in Jewish education is to teach the children Torah (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Talmud Torah 1:1). At the same time, the Sages said that it is a mitzva to teach children a trade from which they can earn a living (Kiddushin 30b; SA OḤ 306:6).

Ideally, the mitzva is upon the parents to teach their children Torah. Unlike in other cultures, in which wisdom belongs to a closed circle of intellectuals, in Israel the Torah belongs to all, as it is said (Devarim 33:4): "Moshe commanded us a Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Ya'akov" – all the descendants of Ya'akov our father belong to the Torah, and all parents must know Torah in order to teach it to their children. And this is because the Torah is not an abstract wisdom detached from reality, but a Torah of life, which directs and straightens a person's way in all the layers of his life. Therefore it is called 'Torah', from the word hora'a, instruction. Accordingly, the parents who gave their children life in the physical sense – who begot him and gave him food, clothing and love – must also give him the spiritual and moral meaning of life, and transmit to him the divine Torah, which is the good gift that the Holy One, blessed be He, gave to Israel.

In practice, because of the burdens of earning a living, parents fulfil a considerable part of the mitzva with the help of teachers and educators in the frameworks of schools and Talmud Torahs. Nevertheless, the mitzva to educate the children remains an obligation upon the parents, while the teachers are only the agents of the parents and do not replace them in responsibility for the mitzva of education. Therefore, the mitzva and obligation is upon the parents to impart to their children the strength of soul and the desire to study Torah, to send them to school joyfully, to encourage them to study, to follow their progress and to keep in contact with the teachers, and to study with the children as far as they are able.

In addition, the foundation of education is personal example. That is, the mitzva of education obligates parents to serve as a positive example for their children, because when the children see that their parents cleave to the Torah and the mitzvot with joy, they want to go in their way. To strengthen this, parents are commanded to talk with their children about the faith and values that guide their lives, to share with them their experience and the choices that stood before them, and to implant in them faith in God and in their special destiny, so that when they grow up they will be able to choose the way that suits them for realising their talent and for the repair of the world.

sections.title_en: How Far One Must Teach One's Son and Daughter
sections.body_en:
In the mitzva of Torah study two commands were stated: one to the parents, that they teach their children Torah, as it is said (Devarim 11:19): "And you shall teach them to your children, to speak of them." The second is directed to the children themselves, that when they grow up they take responsibility upon themselves and study Torah, as it is said (Devarim 5:1): "And you shall learn them and keep them, to do them."

That is, when the children reach the age of education, the parents are commanded to begin educating their children to study the foundations of the Torah, in order to know how to live a Torah life. And from the time the children reach the age of mitzvot, the parents and children become partners in the mitzva, with the primary responsibility to study the foundations of the Torah in order to live a Torah life resting upon the youths, who must be diligent and make an effort to understand the Torah properly, while their parents are commanded to encourage them and educate them for this, and to help with everything needed so that they can complete the obligation of their study. And as long as they have not yet reached the Torah level sufficient to live according to the guidance of the Torah, the parents and the children have not yet fulfilled their mitzva properly (Kiddushin 30a; see Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:4; above 1, note 1).

From the time the son has reached knowledge of the foundations of the Torah in order to live a Torah life, the parents have fulfilled their mitzva. From then on the entire responsibility passes to the shoulders of the children, and they must continue to review their learning and delve into it so that the Torah continues to guide their lives. And if they were negligent and forgot their learning, the responsibility and the blame are theirs. However, if the parents have influence on their adult children, it is a mitzva that they continue to encourage them to engage in Torah, to review their learning and to delve into it (see Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, ibid. 1:6).

According to the guidance of the Sages, one can arrive at knowledge of the foundations of the Torah by the age of twenty, as explained in tractate Avot (5:21): from the age of five to ten they studied Scripture, and from the age of ten to fifteen they studied Mishna, that is, all the decided laws. And from the age of fifteen until twenty they studied Talmud, which is the explanation of the reasons of the laws. After that they devoted themselves to supporting their families, while setting fixed times for Torah in order to review their learning and delve into it (see Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, ibid. 1:1, and 3:4).

However, times have changed. In the time of the Mishna they did not write down the Oral Torah, and even the Written Torah had no vowels or cantillation marks, and therefore they devoted five years to memorising the verses with their correct reading, with vowels and cantillation. After that they devoted five years to studying and memorising by heart the mishnayot, which are the decided laws. And after that they devoted five more years to studying the reasons of the laws in the Gemara and memorising them. But today it has been permitted to print the Torah with vowels and cantillation, and it has likewise been permitted to write down the Oral Torah. Therefore, on the one hand there is no need to devote so much time to memorising by heart; but on the other hand, over time the opinions and details have multiplied, and it takes a long time to study them, understand them and remember them, and likewise one must know how to study Gemara, that is, the methods of study. But in the final analysis, even today, if the studies were conducted properly, it would be possible to study the foundations of the Torah well by about the age of twenty (see ibid. 1:6).

In practice, in most cases the graduates of the yeshiva ketana and yeshiva high schools do not properly know the foundations of the Torah – in halakha, faith and ethics – as needed to guide their lives, and they also do not know how to study Gemara properly. Therefore, in order that they fulfil the mitzva of Torah study properly, they need to continue studying in yeshiva. And the parents too are commanded to encourage their sons in this and to help them as far as they are able. For as long as their son does not know the foundations of the Torah for halakha and practice, they have not yet fulfilled the mitzva of "And you shall teach them to your children."

As for daughters, although there is no obligation that they study Gemara, there is an obligation that they study the foundations of halakha, faith and ethics, in an explained and deep way, as needed to guide their lives (above 1:17). In practice, generally the girls too do not manage to study, within the framework of the high schools and ulpanot, the foundations of the Torah needed for the guidance of life. Therefore, the girls are commanded to complete the study of the foundations of the Torah through self-study and classes, and sometimes even within the framework of a midrasha. And their parents are commanded to help them in this.

It must be added that in the past, even one who did not study all the foundations of the Torah generally continued in the tradition of the fathers; and although they and their parents did not fulfil the mitzva of study properly, and accordingly could also not guide their lives in the light of the Torah properly, in any case they preserved the Jewish tradition. But in recent generations, in the wake of the challenges of modernity, if the parents do not see to it that their children study the foundations of the Torah, both from the halakhic aspect and from the aspect of faith, there is great concern that they will not be able to preserve even the Jewish tradition.1

notes_en.en: We have learned that there are two parts to the mitzva of Torah study: one, to study what is needed for the guidance of life according to the Torah, as it is said (Devarim 5:1): "And you shall learn them and keep them, to do them", and in this mitzva women are obligated like men. And there is a further mitzva to add and teach the sons the theoretical field, such as Gemara, as it is said (Devarim 11:19): "And you shall teach them to your children." In the past, the study that sufficed for girls to live according to the Torah did not require organised study in a school, for what they learned at home sufficed for most of them, and therefore a system of study was set up only for boys. But today it is clear that girls must study halakha, faith and ethics thoroughly, like the boys, so that they can live according to the Torah, as it is said "And you shall learn them and keep them, to do them" (as explained above 1:17). Accordingly, the Torah obligation to teach the sons today obligates the parents to teach the daughters too everything needed to live a life of Torah and mitzvot.

sections.title_en: Parents' Payment for Their Children's Studies
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, in practice, because of the burden of earning a living, parents make use of teachers in order to teach their children Torah. The question is to what extent the parents are obligated to pay for this. Originally the discussion was regarding sons, both from the aspect of the father, who was responsible for supporting the family, and from the aspect of the son, who needed to study the foundations of the Torah in order to guide his life according to it; therefore we will study this first, and from it we will continue to the obligation regarding daughters. There are three levels of study: a) the study of the Written Torah; b) the study of the Oral Torah; c) seeing to the provision of their needs during the time of their studies. We will detail further:

The first level: learning to read the Written Torah. This payment is an absolute obligation incumbent upon the father. And if the father's financial situation is straitened and he has no money to pay for the son, the leaders of the community are commanded to arrange a possibility for the son to study free of charge. And if they do not do so, the father is obligated to sell his garment or to collect charity in order to hire a teacher to teach him to read the Written Torah.

The second level: the study of the Oral Torah. This payment too is an absolute obligation upon the father, and if he does not want to pay, the beit din compels him to pay. But if he has no money to pay, he is not obligated to collect charity for the study of the Oral Torah by his son, and the responsibility for this passes to the community as a whole and to the Sages of Israel, who are commanded to teach the son of the poor man the Oral Torah without payment.

The third level: providing food, clothing and housing for the son while he is studying the foundations of the Torah in order to live according to its guidance. Indeed, this payment too is included in the obligation to teach the sons Torah, for if they do not have food, clothing and housing, they will not be able to free themselves for Torah study. But since this is not a direct payment for Torah study, the beit din did not intervene to compel the parents to pay for it.

It seems that, as with the second level, so is the law regarding parents' payment for the studies of daughters. That is, parents are obligated to pay for the teachers who teach the girls reading and the foundations needed to live a Torah life, and the parents may even be compelled to pay for this. And although the parents are obligated to pay also for the accompanying expenses of their upkeep during their studies, they are not compelled to do so.2

It must further be known that what parents pay for their obligation to teach their sons and daughters Torah cannot be paid from ma'aser kesafim (the monetary tithe), since this is a mitzva that they are obligated to fulfil, and one may not fulfil a mitzva in which a person is obligated with tithe money. But what one pays for the needs of food, clothing and housing of a son or daughter after the age of eighteen, whom by law one is no longer obligated to support – in a time of need one may pay from the tithe money (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, ibid. 1:7).3

notes_en.en:
The source for the obligation to pay for the study of the Oral Torah, for one who can afford it, is in the words of the Rama"h cited in the Tur YD 245:6, and the SA there cited them, as did Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:4 and 1:7. And there in law 7 the third level is explained. The distinction between the Written Torah and the Oral Torah stems from the fact that in principle one may take money for teaching the Written Torah and not for the Oral Torah; since this is so, it is understood that the obligation to pay for study applies only to the Written Torah and not to the Oral Torah. And since it is an absolute obligation, the father is obligated to do everything to see to it that his son studies the Written Torah. In practice, for the study of the Oral Torah too one pays teachers compensation for their lost time, for if one does not pay, the teachers will have nothing on which to live and will be forced to look for a livelihood and will not teach the youths of Israel. Therefore one who has the ability to pay for the Oral Torah is obligated to pay, and one who does not have it is exempt from collecting charity or selling his garment and the like.
The obligation to pay for the study of daughters follows from what was explained in the previous note, and above 1:17.

However, several Aḥaronim wrote that the support of older sons too – as long as it is not the way of young men of their age to support themselves – the father must provide for them, and accordingly one should not pay for their food and housing from ma'aser kesafim; similarly wrote the Arukh Ha-shulḥan YD 249:7, and Igrot Moshe YD 1:143, and see Tzedaka U-mishpat 6:2. But in a time of need one may count the payment for the dormitory needs of students above the age of eighteen against ma'aser kesafim. And when even more straitened, one may count the dormitory needs after the age of bar mitzva too as ma'aser kesafim.
Ba'alei teshuva where both the father and the son have not yet studied the foundations of the Torah, and the financial situation allows the father to fund the studies of only one of them: although the father is commanded to see to it that his son studies the foundations of the Torah, he must first fund his own studies, because a mitzva incumbent upon oneself takes precedence, and afterwards fund the son's studies. And if the son is sharper in his understanding, he should first fund the son's studies, for through this Torah will increase more in Israel (Kiddushin 29b; SA YD 245:2).

sections.title_en: The Enactment of Yehoshua ben Gamla to Establish Schools
sections.body_en:
One of the important enactments instituted in Israel is the enactment of Yehoshua ben Gamla, through which public education in Israel was established. In order to explain his enactment, we must go back and summarise that the Torah commanded us three commands in connection with Torah study (above 1:2): a) the parents are commanded to teach their children Torah, or to find a teacher to teach them.
b) the children are commanded to study Torah themselves. c) Torah scholars are commanded to teach Torah to students.

As with all the mitzvot, the Written Torah set the mitzvot before us in principle, and further commanded the Sages of Israel to establish enactments and safeguards in order to pave the good way to realising the mitzvot. And so in the matter of Torah study, the principle that emerges from the three mitzvot is that all of Israel must know the Torah, and that parents and rabbis are commanded to act for this. But these principles need frameworks through which this great ideal can be realised. Yehoshua ben Gamla, who lived in the period of the Second Temple, merited to establish the frameworks of study, and enacted and founded the first educational system in the world.

And so it is related in the Talmud (Bava Batra 21a): "May that man be remembered for good, and Yehoshua ben Gamla is his name, for were it not for him the Torah would have been forgotten from Israel. For at first, whoever had a father – he taught him Torah; whoever had no father – did not learn Torah… They enacted that teachers of children be established in Jerusalem… And still, whoever had a father – he would bring him up and teach him; whoever had no father – would not go up and learn. They enacted that they be established in every district, and they would bring them in at the age of sixteen or seventeen, and whoever's teacher became angry with him would rebel against him and leave. Until Yehoshua ben Gamla came and enacted that teachers of children be established in every province and every city, and they would bring them in at the age of six or seven."

One of the central meanings of the enactment is that the responsibility to see to the studies of children whose parents are unable to pay for their studies rests upon the community as a whole. Both those who have children and those who have no children – all must see to it that all the children of the poor families who are unable to pay tuition reach school and study Torah. For this purpose they would collect taxes from all the members of the community, each according to his wealth, and from the community taxes they would fund the needs of the public, including also the studies of the poor children.

So important is this matter of establishing schools that the Sages said that any city in which there is no arrangement of study for children – the members of the other communities must place it under a ban until they set up a school in it. And if they persisted in their obstinacy and did not set up a school, it is fitting to destroy it and disperse its inhabitants among other communities, provided that there be no place in Israel in which children are not taught Torah (Shabbat 119b; Tur and Beit Yosef YD 245:7).

sections.title_en: The Age of Beginning Study and the Length of the Day
sections.body_en:
The beginning of education for Torah study is from the time the child begins to speak, when his father teaches him the verse: "Moshe commanded us a Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Ya'akov" (Devarim 33:4). And afterwards the verse: "Hear O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one" (Devarim 6:4), and as his understanding develops, so they teach him more Torah. Likewise they teach him to read letters, so that he can read a few verses by the time he reaches the age of six or seven (Sukka 42a; Rema YD 245:8).

When he reaches the age of six or seven he should begin studying in school, for so it was established in the enactment of Yehoshua ben Gamla, that at the age of six or seven they begin organised studies (Bava Batra 21a). And the explanation is that an ordinary child begins his studies at the age of six, and if he is weak, they wait for him to grow stronger and bring him into school when he is seven (Tosafot there, s.v. 'ke-ven').

And what the Sages said (Avot 5:21), that at five one begins to study Scripture, means that at the age of five they began teaching him to read a few verses at home or in a framework similar to a kindergarten, but only at the age of six does he enter school for a full order of studies (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:1).

In the past, it was customary to teach the children during the day and a little of the night, close to the Ma'ariv prayer, so that the habits of study would be fixed in their souls (SA YD 245:11; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Talmud Torah 1:1). It is clear that there were breaks for games and the like; likewise the children would help their parents in their work in the field, and in the busy seasons most of the day was devoted to work. But during the rest of the year most of the day was used for study. The studies took place on all the weekdays of the year, and on the eves of Sabbaths and festivals they would shorten the school day in order to prepare for Shabbat and the festival. So it was customary in Israel from the period of the Second Temple until close to our day. Through these intensive studies the Jews were known throughout the world as a wise and understanding people that produces from its midst renowned geniuses.

Upon all of us rests the responsibility to raise education and study to the top of the agenda. In the Jewish talent for study lies enormous potential, and every investment in it is worthwhile. If we invest efforts and resources in education for Torah and science, we will merit to raise and nurture Torah scholars and brilliant scientists, and all the Jews of the world will want to come up to the Land in order to be partners in developing Israeli talent and spiritual creativity. And even the gentiles will say of us: "Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people" (Devarim 4:6). And the vision of the prophets will be fulfilled in us: "And many nations shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Ya'akov, and He will teach us of His ways and we will walk in His paths, for out of Zion shall go forth Torah and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem" (Mikha 4:2).

sections.title_en: The Number of Children in a Class
sections.body_en:
A central question in the subject of education is how many students there should be in each class. In this question two needs collide. From the aspect of study, it is preferable to give each teacher a small class in which every student will receive more attention and nurturing. From the economic side, the more students there are in a class, the smaller the expenses of education will be, and the easier it will be for the parents and the public treasury to fund the teachers' salaries. For example, in a place where the whole age group numbers one hundred and twenty students, if they allot a teacher for every forty students, they can make do with three teachers. And if they determine that no class will number more than twenty-five students, they will need five teachers, each of whom must be paid a full salary, and the costs of education will rise significantly.

Within the enactment an answer was given to this (Bava Batra 21a): that each teacher teach twenty-five students. However, it is not necessary that all the students be of one year group; rather, one class may contain two year groups, and sometimes they were even accustomed to put three year groups into one class, the main thing being that their level of study be more or less equal, so that it will be possible to teach them together.

The poskim disagree when the number of students is above twenty-five. Some say that if the number of students is between twenty-six and forty, they add an assistant to help the teacher, and so together they can teach all the children well. And if there are forty-one children, they divide them into two classes, and each class has its own teacher (Rambam, Nimukei Yosef, SA YD 245:15).

And some say that one teacher suffices for a class whose size is between twenty-five and thirty-nine students. And if there are forty to forty-nine students, they need a teacher and an assistant. And if there are fifty students in the class, they need two teachers (Rosh, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam). In a time of need one may be lenient according to this opinion, provided that one sees that the teacher succeeds in teaching the students (Shakh 245:10).4

Residents of small settlements who do not have enough children to maintain a class must send their children to the neighbouring settlement, and there they will study in regular classes. And although in the enactment of Yehoshua ben Gamla it was determined that one does not send children from place to place, that is on condition that it is possible to set up a regular class in their place; but in a place where there are not enough students for a regular class of close to twenty-five students, they must send them to study in the neighbouring settlement (Bava Batra 21a; and see Emunat Shmuel 26).

And if the matter is impossible, because the neighbouring settlement is too far, or because of the danger of the roads, the residents of that place are obligated to set up a school in their settlement even for a few students, for it cannot be that there should be a place in which the children of Israel do not study Torah. According to the enactment of the Sages, the responsibility for this rests both upon the parents and upon the public as a whole (see Rema ḤM 163, end of 3; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:3).

notes_en.en: The Shakh 245:10 mentioned the opinion of those who are lenient and wrote in practice: "It seems that in this one goes according to the teacher and according to the boys, whether they learn little or much, and everything according to the matter." And some say that in practice one sees that for most teachers and students it is not good to study in a class whose size is above twenty-five students (Emunat Shmuel 26). However, one should consider the change in study hours: in the past the teacher would teach his students most of the hours of the day, and therefore it was hard for him to teach a large group; and perhaps today, when teachers teach fewer hours, they are able to invest more effort in those hours and teach a larger class.

sections.body_en:
A great responsibility rests upon the teachers of Israel. The spiritual future of the people of Israel depends on them. And in fact the future of the whole world depends on them, for Israel among the nations is like the heart among the organs. Therefore the teachers must do their work faithfully, begin the lesson on time, not leave for their own affairs in the middle of the lesson, not talk or send messages on the mobile phone, and all the more so not cancel a lesson. And of every teacher who is negligent in his role, Scripture says: "Cursed be he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully" (Yirmeyahu 48:10; Bava Batra 21b). Therefore one should appoint a teacher who is God-fearing, accomplished in his learning, and who knows how to teach quickly and precisely (SA YD 245:17).

If no teacher is found who is both quick and precise, but one can choose either a teacher who is precise and slow, or one who is quick but sometimes errs in his words, one should prefer the slow and precise teacher over the quick one who is not precise (Bava Batra 21a; SA there 19).

The teacher must be careful not to stay awake many hours at night, lest he be tired when he needs to teach. Likewise he should take care to eat in an orderly way, not too much and not too little, so that he will not be tired or weak and can teach well. If the teacher sleeps too little at night, or he afflicts his body, and because of this he does not teach properly, he should be dismissed and another teacher found who will do his work faithfully (Rema YD 245:17).

It is obligatory to choose the best teacher for the children, and if they found an average teacher, and in the course of time the possibility opened to hire a teacher better than him, one should hire the better one (SA there 18). In periods when every teacher had the possibility of earning a living from working in his field or in a trade he had learned from his fathers, and only because he was asked to teach did he leave his work, when a teacher better than him was found, there was no problem in his returning to his work while the better teacher took his place. But today, when professional training takes a long time, and a person cannot suddenly change his livelihood, and there are employment agreements, according to halakha one cannot suddenly dismiss a teacher and throw him into the street without a livelihood. In any case, one must find the suitable arrangement by which the students will receive the best teacher, and the previous teacher will receive compensation and help for the purpose of professional retraining. (See further Peninei Halakha, Ha-am Ve-ha'aretz 6:12-13, on whether teachers of sacred and secular studies may strike.)

sections.title_en: The Celebration at the Start of Study
sections.body_en:
Many are accustomed to hold a celebration for a son when he reaches the age of three, in honour of his entry into the stage in which they begin to educate him for Torah and mitzvot. As part of the celebration they cut his hair in the haircut of an adult, while taking care not to remove the pe'ot (sidelocks), which it is forbidden to shave. In this way they educate him in the mitzva "You shall not round the corners of your head" (Vayikra 19:27), whose meaning is not to cut the hair of the head in a circle while cutting off the pe'ot. And they found a hint to this in the mitzva of orla, for the Sages said (Tanḥuma Kedoshim 14) of the three years of orla that they hint at the first three years of the infant who does not know how to speak and converse, when no mitzvot are fulfilled with him. "And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, for praise to the Lord" (Vayikra 19:24) – that his father sanctifies him to Torah. And so the holders of this custom learned that in the first three years he is like an orla tree and his hair is not cut, and in the fourth year, when he can already be sanctified, they cut his hair and leave him pe'ot, and this is one of the first mitzvot that are fulfilled with him. This mitzva is special in that through it it is recognisable that the child is a Jew. And since with this mitzva they begin to educate him in mitzvot, it became customary to rejoice in it in order to make the mitzvot beloved, and they invite relatives and friends and serve them food and drink. Some are accustomed to go to a rabbi and involve him in cutting the child's hair, and to ask him to bless the child that he merit blessing in his study. However, there is no obligation to keep the custom of the celebration and the haircut at the age of three, and in practice many do not keep them (and see Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 5:6, on the custom of cutting on Lag Ba-omer close to the age of three).

In many communities they began at the age of three to teach the child to read letters, and they would coat a tablet of letters with honey or sugar and tell him to lick the sweetness on the letters, in order to make the letters and study beloved to him.

On the day the children entered study, at the age of five or six, it was customary to dress the children in beautiful clothes and hold a festive celebration for them with sweets. And some would then give them the letters to lick.

So too today it is customary to hold a festive celebration upon the students' entry into first grade. After a few months, when most of the first-grade children already know how to read, they hold another celebration, a 'siddur party', at which they give them a siddur and begin to accustom them to pray from it. Another celebration is held towards the end of the year, close to the festival of Shavuot – a 'Ḥumash party', at which they distribute to the children the Ḥumash in which they will begin the study of the Written Torah. Many accompany these celebrations with songs and dances, words of blessing and the distribution of sweets.5

notes_en.en: The Orḥot Ḥayim wrote (3): "The custom that our Rabbis of blessed memory followed when they place their sons in Torah study: it is customary, when a person places his son in Torah study, that they write the letters on parchment or on a tablet, and they wash him and dress him in clean clothes, and knead for him ḥallot in honey and milk, and bring him fruits and kinds of delicacies. And they hand him over to a Torah scholar to lead him to the school, and they feed him from the ḥallot in honey and milk and from the fruits and kinds of delicacies, and they have him read the letters. And afterwards they cover them with honey and tell him to lick the honey off the letters, and afterwards they return him to his mother. And when he begins to study Torah, they begin with Torat Kohanim in the book of Vayikra, and they make him a festive meal, for it seems to his father as if he were bringing him to Mount Sinai." This custom is already brought in Maḥzor Vitry 508, and likewise in the Roke'aḥ, Shavuot 296, and in the Kol Bo 74.

sections.body_en:
While the children are small, it is a Torah mitzva upon their parents to teach them Torah and to accustom them to keep its mitzvot. However, the obligation of actually fulfilling each and every mitzva is rabbinic (as explained in halakha 1). And from the time they grow up and are able to take responsibility for their actions, they are obligated to keep the mitzvot by Torah law: the daughter from the age of twelve and the son from the age of thirteen (Nidda 45b; SA OḤ 616:2). And this matter is founded on a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai (Rosh, Maharil).

The Sages said that from the moment a person is born until he reaches the age of mitzvot he has the evil inclination within him, and from the moment he reaches the age of mitzvot the good inclination also enters him (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 16; Zohar Ḥadash 1:18; Zohar 2:98a).

Seemingly one should ask: the infant and the child appear sweet and good, so why did the Sages say that they have only an evil inclination? And conversely, it is precisely adolescents who are beginning to mature who sometimes tend to be insolent and to cast off the yoke, so how did the Sages say that precisely then the good inclination enters them?

But the essence of the good inclination comes to expression in a person's ability to understand the world and to choose to do good deeds in order to repair it, whereas the minor is occupied with concern for himself, without the ability to understand the world and to choose to act for its repair. Even when the minor does good deeds he generally does them in order to win prizes or compliments, or refrains from an action out of fear of punishment. This is the meaning of the evil inclination present in the minor – an inclination that is concerned for itself. And when he begins to mature, the good inclination also enters him, and from now on he is able to take responsibility and to do good to the world.

However, since until the age of twenty the boys and girls have not yet completed their process of maturing, they find it harder to overcome their inclination and to defer gratification, and they are more liable to err and be tempted. Therefore, until the age of twenty a person is not judged in the heavenly court for his sins with full severity (Shabbat 89b). But since from the time they reach the age of mitzvot they are basically able to be responsible for their actions, they become obligated in the mitzvot and become partners in the responsibility of all Israel for keeping the Torah and the mitzvot. Therefore they can be agents for fulfilling mitzvot, such as testifying about the immersion of vessels, or fulfil the obligation of others in their mitzvot, such as by saying Kiddush on Shabbat and lighting the Ḥanukka candles for the family; and likewise, if they eat, they can recite the blessing aloud and fulfil the obligation of those who hear them (Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 1:10).6

notes_en.en:
It is explained in the Mishna in Nidda 45b, and this is also the opinion of Rebbi, that a girl of twelve becomes obligated in mitzvot, whereas the boy at the age of thirteen, and this is because the Holy One, blessed be He, gave "extra understanding to the woman more than to the man", and therefore she becomes obligated in mitzvot a year earlier. And according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, the son becomes obligated in mitzvot at the age of twelve and the daughter at the age of thirteen, and this is because it is customary to send the son to study Torah and a trade, and therefore "cunning (worldly wisdom) enters him first." And even if he has no rabbi and teacher, since he is accustomed to go out and come in, because of this he becomes sharper than the daughter, who is not accustomed to go out of her home (Tosafot there). And the halakha is that daughters enter into mitzvot a year earlier, according to the opinion of Rebbi (SA OḤ 616:2). The foundation of this halakha, that the time of obligation in mitzvot arrives at the age of adolescence, is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai (see Responsa of the Rosh 16:1; Rashbatz on Avot 5:21; Responsa Maharil 51; Tiferet Yisrael, Avot 5:161; MB 55:40).
Likewise regarding all Israel being guarantors for one another (Sanhedrin 43b; Rashi on Devarim 29:28): from the time they reach the age of mitzvot they enter into this guarantorship, and they can be agents for a matter of mitzva and fulfil the obligation of another Jew (SA OḤ 55:9; EH 169:10; ḤM 35:3).
In order to fulfil another's obligation or to be appointed as an agent, one must reach the age of mitzvot and the first two hairs must begin to grow as a sign of maturity. However, in the Talmud (Nidda 48b) the words of Rava are brought, that one need not examine a girl who has reached the age of twelve as to whether she can perform mi'un (refusal), because there is a presumption that she has brought forth two hairs. And the conclusion of the Gemara is that this law was stated only for stringency, such as to prevent her from performing mi'un, but for leniency, that she can perform ḥalitza in a case where she fell to yibum, one does not rely on the presumption, and in order for her ḥalitza to be valid one must examine that she has brought forth signs. In practice the poskim disagree about the force of the presumption: some say that one relies on the presumption in every matter except in matters concerning Torah laws of forbidden relations (Maharik, Ḥadashim 47). And some say that even in forbidden relations one relies on it, except for ḥalitza, where the Sages said one must examine (Zera Emet 3, YD 142). And according to most poskim, for all Torah laws, such as fulfilling another's obligation in Birkat Ha-mazon and the reading of Parashat Zakhor, one must examine, but for rabbinic matters such as prayer and blessings one relies on the presumption (MA 55:7; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 6; MB 31). And some say that even in their opinion, by Torah law one relies on the presumption, and only the Sages said that in Torah laws one should not rely on the presumption. Therefore, after the fact, if a boy who wrote tefillin is no longer before us, one relies on the presumption that since he reached the age of thirteen, it is presumed that he brought forth hairs (Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana OḤ 1; Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham 55:7; Torat Ḥesed OḤ 1). And it is possible that when great humiliation would be caused by the examination, one should rely on their opinion on the presumption even in Torah laws, such as to fulfil another's obligation in Kiddush.

sections.title_en: The Celebration of Bar and Bat Mitzva
sections.body_en:
It is a great joy for a son and daughter of Israel who reach the age at which they become obligated in mitzvot, for the Sages said (Bava Kamma 87a): "Greater is one who is commanded and does than one who is not commanded and does", for since he is more bound to the mitzva, his reward for fulfilling it is greater. Therefore it is a mitzva to hold a meal in honour of the entry into mitzvot, which is a joy of cleaving to the mitzvot.

It is customary that during the meal the one entering the yoke of mitzvot stands before the gathering and thanks God for the privilege of becoming obligated in mitzvot and of being a partner in the great destiny of the people of Israel, and adds words of Torah as an expression of his having become a full partner in the responsibility for keeping the Torah. And the parents too thank God for having merited to raise their child and bring him to this (Yam shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma 7:37; MB 225:6). Likewise it is customary that Torah scholars or relatives say words of Torah at the meal and bless the one entering into mitzvot.

And so it is related in the Zohar (Zohar Ḥadash 1:18b) that Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai invited the masters of the Mishna to eat at a great meal that he made, and he was exceedingly joyful. The guests asked him why he was so joyful, and he answered: because on this day my son Elazar has reached the age of thirteen, and a holy soul (neshama) descends upon him. The meaning is that until the age of thirteen only the nefesh is revealed in him, whereas from the age of thirteen he can receive the neshama as well, and this is the meaning of accepting the yoke of mitzvot and the entry of the good inclination. And the celebration that Avraham our father made for Yitzḥak our father too – some explain that it was on the day he reached bar mitzva, as it is said (Bereshit 21:8): "And the child grew and was weaned, and Avraham made a great feast on the day that Yitzḥak was weaned." "Weaned" (higamel) means that he was weaned from servitude to the evil inclination and the good inclination entered him (Bereshit Rabba 53:10, according to Matnot Kehuna). From this meal a great advocacy is awakened on behalf of Israel, "that the advocates of righteousness say before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the world, see Your children, how joyful they are that they are entering the yoke of Your mitzvot" (Ben Ish Ḥai, Re'eh 17).

It is a mitzva to hold the meal on the very day of entry into mitzvot, which is the twelfth birthday for daughters and the thirteenth for sons, and that is the true day of rejoicing. When it is difficult to hold the meal on the birthday itself, one may hold it a day or two afterwards, since the joy of the day of entry into mitzvot still continues; however, in order to strengthen the mitzva in the meal even though it is not on the day of entry into mitzvot, one should increase words of Torah in it (see Yam shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma 7:37; MA 225:4). And it is good that the bar or bat mitzva make a 'siyum' of an important book at it.

It is good to buy a new garment for the son or daughter reaching mitzvot, so that they may recite 'She-heḥeyanu' over it, and have in mind also to give thanks for their entry that day into the yoke of mitzvot (Ben Ish Ḥai, Re'eh 17). Even when one is forced to postpone the celebration by a day or two, it is good that they recite 'She-heḥeyanu' over a new garment on the birthday on which they enter into mitzvot.

Parents who are meticulous in the mitzva are accustomed to study with the boy or girl, towards their entry into mitzvot, about the meaning of the Torah and the acceptance of the mitzvot. And some are meticulous to arrange a journey for their child in which he will deepen his acquaintance with the roots of the family, the grandfathers and grandmothers, and in this way they connect his private joy to the glorious chain of generations of the Jewish people. And some are accustomed to have him meet Torah scholars, or Jews who are engaged in important mitzvot such as settling the Land, education, helping others or scientific developments for the benefit of humanity, and in this way they connect personal responsibility for keeping the mitzvot to national responsibility and to the repair of the world. Similarly it is related in tractate Soferim (18:7) that the people of Jerusalem would take their sons, when they entered into mitzvot, to be blessed by Torah scholars. Some are accustomed that the boy or girl presents the impressions of the journey at the meal of entry into mitzvot.

There were those who argued against the celebration of a bat mitzva, that it is a custom that did not exist in the past in Israel, and that keeping it involves imitating the customs of the gentiles and breaching the bounds of modesty. And perhaps in the past there was a basis for their argument, but today there is no room to be concerned for their words. For in the distant past, apart from individuals who were meticulous in this, in most families they were also not accustomed to hold a bar mitzva celebration for boys. Apparently, because of poverty and the burden of work, they did not multiply celebrations where they were not obligated. But since it is right to celebrate the day of entry into mitzvot, in recent generations, when the burden of work has lessened and people have become wealthier and are able more easily to fund a celebration and to free the time required to take part in it, the custom of the bar mitzva celebration has spread throughout Israel. And since in the past the accepted practice in the world was that women went out of their homes less and were more retiring, the bat mitzva too was marked only within the family, by buying a new and festive garment (Ben Ish Ḥai, Year One, Re'eh 17). However, as women began to go out more to various occupations and to take responsibility also for public affairs, so the need to celebrate the day of their entry into mitzvot with a large celebration grew, until the custom of celebrating a bat mitzva with a se'udat mitzva became widespread (Seridei Esh 3:93; Yaskil Avdi 5, OḤ 28; Yabia Omer 6, OḤ 29). Moreover, in our time it is usual to celebrate various occasions, such as a birthday and an end-of-school-year party; if so, all the more so should one celebrate the birthday on which one enters into mitzvot.

Therefore, it is a mitzva to celebrate the day of the daughter's entry into mitzvot. And just as they prepare the boys to read and study Torah towards the bar mitzva, so it is right to prepare the girls to study Torah and to prepare a derasha on the value of the Torah and the mitzvot towards the bat mitzva. And if possible, it is good that the daughter study a book of halakha or another important book and complete it at the celebration.

It is an ancient custom from the period of the Rishonim that the boy is called up to the Torah on the first Shabbat after he reaches mitzvot (Minhagei Maharil, Keri'at Ha-Torah 5), and it is customary to call him up for the 'maftir' aliya so that he reads the haftara. In recent generations some are accustomed that the boy prepares the whole parasha and reads it before the congregation, and by virtue of this he learns to be a 'ba'al korei'. But one must make an effort that the burden of the reading not weigh too heavily on him and cast a shadow over the joy of entering into mitzvot. Likewise one must check whether the bar mitzva boy has reached a fitting level for reading the Torah, for if not, it is not in keeping with the dignity of the congregation that he read for everyone; moreover, it is likely that he will make such errors on account of which he must be made to repeat, and if they make him repeat for every error, the boy will be caused grief and shame, and if they do not make him repeat, the congregation will not have fulfilled the obligation of the Torah reading.

The custom of Ashkenaz is that the father recites a blessing when his son reaches the age of mitzvot: "Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who has exempted me from the punishment of this one." And so wrote the Rishonim of Ashkenaz (Itur 3, Hilkhot Mila; Tashbetz Katan 390; Minhagei Maharil, Keri'at Ha-Torah 5). The source of this blessing is in the midrash (Bereshit Rabba 63:10; Pesikta Zutarta, Toledot 25). The meaning of the blessing is that until the age of thirteen the father is responsible for the actions of his son and is punished for them, and from now on the son is responsible for his actions. And some explain that until the age of mitzvot, since the children are not responsible for their actions, if they undergo suffering it is because of the sin of their parents, and therefore the father recites a blessing when they reach mitzvot for being exempted from this responsibility.

However, in many communities of Sephardic origin they were not accustomed to recite this blessing, which is not mentioned in the Talmud. And even in Ashkenaz there were those who were accustomed to say it without the Divine Name and Kingship, in such a way that it is not considered a blessing but a thanksgiving.

In practice there are three customs in this: a) the custom of many of Ashkenazic origin is to say the blessing with the Divine Name and Kingship (Gra 225:3; Ḥayei Adam 65:3; Olat Re'iya). And the widespread custom is to say the blessing after the completion of the bar mitzva's first aliya to the Torah.

b) The custom of many of Ashkenazic origin and of Sephardic origin is to say the blessing without the Divine Name and Kingship. Those of Ashkenazic origin say it after the aliya to the Torah, and those of Sephardic origin at the meal (Rema OḤ 225:2, Levush, Derekh Ha-ḥayim; Ben Ish Ḥai, Re'eh 17; Yabia Omer 6, OḤ 29).

c) The custom of many who came from North Africa and Yemen and other Sephardic communities is not to say this blessing at all (Zokher Brit Avot p. 30; Alei Hadas 18:9; Keter Shem Tov p. 318).

Putting on tefillin: Regarding education in all the mitzvot the rule is that from the time the minor can understand the rules of the mitzva and fulfil it according to halakha – each mitzva according to its complexity and the difficulty of fulfilling it – they educate him to fulfil it (Sukka 42a; MB 343:3; Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 24:1). And some act in this way also regarding tefillin, and from the time the father assesses that his son is able to keep his body clean, he begins to educate him to put on tefillin. However, the widespread custom is to postpone the education for tefillin until close to the bar mitzva. And this is because putting on tefillin must be done with reverence, while keeping a clean body and without distraction, and it is hard to educate children in this. In practice, some are accustomed that the boy begins to put on tefillin a month before the bar mitzva, and some do so earlier and put them on two or three months before the bar mitzva. And some are accustomed to mark the beginning of the fulfilment of the mitzva with a festive event.
